The bar had overflow-x-auto so it could scroll when tight, and a scrolling row is a clipping container: the panels opened and were invisible, clipped by the bar they hung from. And three category buttons plus the utility rail do not fit a phone at all. So the bar never scrolls, and below md it becomes one button carrying every category as a heading - two renderings again, but both read app_nav_groups and a shared item partial, so they cannot disagree about what exists or how the current page is marked, only about how many buttons carry it.

ADR-0041 decision 5, and the finding that reframed it: the platform was never document-free. CandidateProfile has accepted a resume and portfolio files since SPEC-0029, under a content-type allowlist, a ten-megabyte ceiling, candidate-owned export, and a delete that removes attachments before the row. So the question was not what a document contract should say - most of it was already written - but what internship records may attach and what that contract did not cover: scanning, a retention clock, and post-internship access. The user answered all four questions. A request shares the resume rather than storing one: resume_shared_at is a timestamp, not a blob, because a second copy would mean two retention clocks and two deletions for the one document the platform is least entitled to duplicate, and it would break the promise that deleting a resume from a profile deletes it everywhere - which a test now pins. A deliverable is a new record because the work a student produces during a placement had no home anywhere. The safety envelope is SPEC-0029's, reused rather than reinvented, and nothing is scanned - which is exactly why the other half matters more: this is the first path in the application by which one person reads a file another person uploaded, so every download is served by an app route as an attachment under nosniff, with the content type re-identified by Active Storage rather than trusted from the uploader, and never through a signed blob URL, because a signed URL authorizes the link rather than the reader and outlives both the placement and the membership that justified it. Access ends with its record: a company reads a shared resume while the request is open and while the internship it produced runs, never after a rejection or completion, and reads deliverables only while the placement is open. The faculty supervisor was offered a reader's seat and the user declined it - the assignment grants the placement and its weekly reports, not the student's files. The student deletes their own work and nothing expires on a timer. Two things came out of building it rather than specifying it: the model's transition! leaves a record dirty on status after it syncs, so a plain update! for the sharing stamp was refused by the guard that catches untracked status changes - it uses update_columns now, the same idiom acknowledgement already used - and opening the screen showed the request notice still promising no resume or file uploads, which the same page now disproved. That copy is corrected in both locales, and the two places the ADR and spec still said text only are marked superseded rather than quietly edited.

bin/rails test:spec[SPEC-0041] reads a lifecycle document's enforced_by and runs exactly those files, so the rule recorded this morning is a command rather than a copy-paste from a doc. It works on decision records too, names the system tests instead of running them because they are the slow half that belongs to the gate, and refuses with a useful message when a spec lists nothing - an empty enforced_by is the actual bug, and the fix is to fill it in rather than to run everything. It shells out rather than calling Rake::Task[test].invoke: the Rails test task takes its files from the command line, so invoking it in process quietly ran all 1,204 tests, which is the one thing the task exists to avoid. Alongside it, the two dead ends the route sweep found are closed. A dismissed job recommendation can be brought back: the undo action had existed since job discovery shipped with nothing linking to it, so a misclick hid a recommendation permanently for anyone who did not know the route. And the company internship-applications index is gone rather than linked - it had no template at all, so an authorized reader would have met a missing-template error, while the program's own screen already lists its applications with the decide and evaluate controls on them. The one test that used that route to prove cross-organization refusal now proves it through the accept action, which is the stronger assertion.

The company internship-applications index removed earlier today was one instance of a class: a route that exists, resolves, and is a 500 waiting for its first authorized visitor, because the action has no template and nothing links to it. test/operations/route_reachability_test.rb closes the class. It asserts every route resolves to an action that exists, and that every GET either renders a template or appears in WITHOUT_TEMPLATE with a sentence saying why - nine do today, all of them send_data or a partial, each now named. Writing it was a lesson in the repo's own rule that a test must fail for the intended reason before it is trusted: the first version passed against a deliberately planted template-less route, because it decided an action was safe by reading forty lines from the method definition and swept up a render from the next method down. The second version read only the method's own body and then produced two false positives - policies#privacy and #terms are endless methods delegating to a private show that renders, and both answer 200. Source-sniffing cannot decide this, so the heuristic is gone: a template-less GET is now a written exception rather than a guess, which is also the version that fails loudly when the next one appears. Both defect shapes were planted and confirmed failing before the test was kept. Registered in the agent-flow invariant table and in the CLAUDE.md invariant list, because a rule not written as a test does not exist.

bundler-audit went red on a run that had passed an hour earlier, and nothing in this repository had changed to cause it: the ruby-advisory-db refreshed at 02:25 with two new entries. CVE-2026-66066 is arbitrary file read and remote code execution in Active Storage variant processing, against activestorage 8.1.3; CVE-2026-71847 is a use-after-free in JSON::ResumableParser on truncated duplicate-key streams, against json 2.21.1. Rails is now 8.1.3.1 and json 2.21.2, both the versions the advisories name, taken conservatively so nothing else moved. The application builds no variants anywhere - a grep finds no .variant call - so the exposure was narrower than the title suggests, but the repository treats a security scan as a gate rather than as advice and the fix is a patch release. Worth noting for its own sake: this is the second time today the timing mattered more than the content. A gate is only as good as the day it last ran, and this one would have blocked the build for anyone who pulled main tomorrow morning without touching a line of it.

SPEC-0041 ships four increments and a fresh database showed none of them: no request to decide, no placement to advance, no week to acknowledge, no supervisor, no file. Every screen built over the last two days was an empty state, which is the one thing a demo cannot demonstrate. The seeds now walk one internship the whole way - a student's request, a shared resume, the company's approval, an active placement, a weekly report, an administrator-assigned supervisor, and a deliverable - through the real APIs rather than written straight into the tables, so the seeded rows are the ones the app itself would produce, guards and all. The replant caught the ordering error immediately: sharing a resume is only allowed while a request is open, and the first version shared it after approval. It had passed in development because the flag was already set there by hand, which is exactly the kind of thing a wiped database is for. Two replants in a row produce the same single set of rows.

A defect introduced this morning by INT-006 and caught by measuring rather than by reading: the placement screen filtered deliverables with a per-record readable_by?, and the company half of that rule is two membership lookups, so the screen cost two queries per file. Measured at seven queries for one deliverable and fifteen for five - it grew with the pile, which is exactly what test/models/query_budget_test.rb and the agent-flow invariant table already forbid for a cohort. InternshipPlacement#deliverables_readable_by asks the company question once and returns a scope: the whole list for a decider while the placement is open, and the author's own otherwise, which is the same rule readable_by? states for one record. The budget test now covers it, and the regression was planted and confirmed failing at seven versus twenty-five queries before the fix was kept. Seeding the internship exposed a second, older trap the repository had already documented in test/fixtures/organizations.yml: a table the seeds write and the fixtures do not name is never cleared between them, so a seeded row outlives the users it points at and the next fixture load dies on a foreign key. Eight tables needed the same deliberately-empty file - the five internship tables, candidate profiles, and both Active Storage tables - and the note in each says why it is empty.

The roadmap and the backlog disagreed in both directions at once, and nothing read both files. The UTCC summary table still called five finished milestones Next or Later, and the consolidated table still described the Student Internship Request Platform as increments 1 to 3 after increment 4 had shipped. The roadmap is what a person opens to decide what to build next, so a stale cell sends somebody to build what already exists or to leave alone what nobody has started. script/validate-backlog, already a gate through bin/docs, now reads docs/roadmap.md as well: a milestone the backlog tracks is Complete on the roadmap exactly when every one of its items is complete, checked in the consolidated table, the summary table, and each milestone section status line. Milestones with no backlog items — the M0 baseline and the unaccepted proposals M12, M13, M14 — have nothing to compare and are left alone.

Ecosystem M13 is order 3 in the unified plan and had no ADR and no specification, so the roadmap gate had nothing to confirm or refuse. Writing them turned up why: the proposal intake it proposes to extend has no governing document either, and three of its four statuses are unreachable. Nothing in app/ assigns status, there is no index or review screen, and the author-facing page renders a status that can never change. M13's stated outcome is the proportion of proposals receiving an auditable decision and an author-visible explanation; that proportion is zero by construction, so the baseline the roadmap defers to discovery is already known. ADR-0049 is proposed, not accepted: record the existing boundary first, make the first increment triage rather than participation, keep the audience as it is, and keep the explanation in-app because ADR-0004 still defers production email. SPEC-0049 is a draft record of the shipped intake, naming the dead statuses as a defect rather than a design. No code changed and no M13 delivery item exists.

Writing SPEC-0049 showed that the proposal intake's two refusals were the two things no test touched: one contributor reading another's proposal, and an incomplete submission re-rendering the form. Each is one line of controller, which is exactly how they get lost. Both hold, and are now asserted along with a staff account being turned away from the form. That third test is where the draft specification turned out to be wrong: a signed-in account with the wrong role is redirected to root with the forbidden flash, not refused outright, because Authorization#authorize_role lands both of its denials there. The specification now says so. The one gap left open is deliberate: that no code path changes status cannot be usefully asserted until ADR-0049 decision 6 settles the status vocabulary, since either form of the assertion would be deleted by the change that answers it.

bin/docs warned about 28 documents past review_by on every run, which is how a warning stops being read. Most of it was not debt: 19 are accepted documents past a mechanical created-plus-seven stamp, and 4 are correctly draft because their work is genuinely blocked - ADR-0010 and SPEC-0010 for UTCC SSO, ADR-0022 and SPEC-0022 for production deployment, which the backlog already records as M6-002 and M9-004. The real finding was 4 documents whose frontmatter contradicted their own bodies. M7-001 and M7-002 shipped on 2026-08-03 with the approval recorded in this file in the user's own words, their specs carry enforced_by lists pointing at tests that exist and pass, and their review-state blockquotes say the user approved them - while status still said draft, and the README index said draft too, so nothing could catch it. ADR-0012, ADR-0013, SPEC-0012, and SPEC-0013 now record the acceptance that happened, with the date it was recorded kept distinct from the date it was given. SPEC-0015 was deliberately left as draft: its work is complete and its tests pass too, but its own text says it remains blocked on the unreviewed supported-flag rows, scopes, runtime consumers, and academic policy, so any rule that swept it up with the others would have been wrong.

bin/docs printed 28 identical review_by lines on every run, and reading 28 identical lines is how DOCS-014's finding stayed hidden: four documents whose work had shipped nine days earlier, sitting in the same undifferentiated list as nineteen accepted documents a week past a mechanical stamp. The two are now counted and phrased apart. A draft or proposed document past its review date is stalled and names its owners, because it is waiting on a person. Anything else past its date is due for re-review, because it is waiting on the calendar. Neither aborts the build; a decision nobody has made yet is a fact about the project, not a broken gate. The output went from 28 undifferentiated warnings to 5 stalled and 19 due for re-review, and the 5 are a clean cross-check on the backlog: ADR-0010 and SPEC-0010 are M6-002, ADR-0022 and SPEC-0022 are M9-004, and SPEC-0015 is the feature-flag specification deliberately left draft by DOCS-014. Run before today's flip it would have listed 9, and the 4 extra would have been the ones nobody had noticed.

A timestamp in the future is how this file stops being a record and starts being a plan, and it was introduced here by hand today: writing several entries in one sitting and spacing them half an hour apart to keep them ordered walked DEV-006, DOCS-014, and DEV-007 past the clock, so each claimed to be finished before it was. Those three are corrected to 10:25, 10:45, and 11:00, and the top-level updated_at with them. The ordering instinct was right and the method was wrong: updates is not sorted and does not need to be, so an entry never has to be dated later than the one above it. script/validate-backlog now warns on any item or update timestamp in the future and errors on one that will not parse at all. It warns rather than aborts because 19 timestamps across 8 items from earlier sessions are still ahead of the clock, by an hour for DEV-002 through OPS-002 and by up to twenty for INT-005, OPS-001, and UX-007. Whether those clocks were wrong or the entries were deliberately post-dated is for whoever wrote them; the check asks on every run instead of nobody asking.

Recorded a diagnosis, not a fix. Chasing the /maintenance 404 after a push showed the whole documentation site is frozen: it serves a backlog stamped 2026-08-07T22:51:23 and a build stamp of commit 37b6250d, a 2026-08-08 merge into agent/recruitment-platform-vertical-slices. Probing by document age gives a clean cutoff - everything created on or before 2026-08-07 serves 200, everything after it 404s, including all of M11-SIR and both documents written today. The cause is two separate failures on the hosting side. GitHub Actions is locked for billing, so every pages.yml run fails in nine seconds without starting a step, and one earlier run titled 'fix: unbreak the dashboard deploy' failed the same way while looking like a code problem. Vercel is building a branch that is not main. The repository builds clean at 293748f through every gate the deploy runs. Two consequences worth carrying: this item cannot be fixed from the codebase, and every evidence_url in this file currently resolves to nothing, because script/validate-backlog checks that a URL looks like a rendered page and never fetches it.

Diagnosing OPS-001 showed this file's evidence links had been resolving to nothing since 2026-08-07 with no check noticing, because the check read their shape and stopped: a URL ending in .html passed whether or not any document stood behind it. Fetching them would tie the build to a deploy it does not control, which is the wrong trade. The half that is ours is checkable offline - the site is built from docs/, so specs/spec-x.html is a promise that docs/spec-x.md exists, and validate-markdown-graph already holds every Markdown link to exactly that rule. Backlog evidence was the one link surface without it, on both evidence[].url and evidence_url. All 122 relative links resolve today, so a passing run proved nothing and the rule was tested against injected breakage instead: two invented links, one on an item and one on an update, both caught by name. This is a guard rather than a repair. It does nothing for the outage - those links still resolve to nothing in practice until the GitHub billing lock clears - but the next bad link now fails at the gate instead of silently, which is the same reasoning as the route reachability invariant: close the class, not the instance.

An audit of app/services found the one real defect it produced. ADR-0037 suppresses application totals and status cells below five, and its fitness function says counts below the threshold are suppressed consistently; the code decided it on the total alone, so once the total cleared five every per-status cell published its exact count. Six applications, five submitted and one screening, produced a cell of one and named the single person who had reached screening to a reader who can see who applied - while the line under the table told them populations below five were suppressed. Suppressing the cell alone would have hidden nothing, because five published beside a total of six returns the sixth by subtraction, so the total is withheld whenever any cell is. Zero is still published: a cell of zero names nobody and hiding it would redact six of seven statuses. All four existing tests passed unmodified, which is the better evidence that this restored the recorded intent rather than bending it.

ADR-0048 records that four counts run on each page load. Measured, the work surface cost 20 queries when application figures were suppressed and 27 when they were not: the four are the dashboard's own, and underneath them OrganizationReporting counted once per status across vocabularies of six and seven while postings asked each relation twice. Thirteen now, on both paths, by grouping the counts - every number on the board survived, so the ADR's prescribed remedy of caching does not apply either. Nothing had guarded this screen; the query budget covered the instructor report, the roster, the catalog, standings and deliverables and stopped there. The new ceiling was measured rather than guessed, by forcing the assertion to fail once to read the true number.

JobAlertNotifier and Observability::Instrumentation had no test anywhere. The first decides whether a student hears about new matches and how often, so the rule that stops a daily alert firing twice - a lock, a re-read of alerts_due? inside it, and a timestamp written only when a notification was created - was resting on nothing. The second is three global subscribers installed from an initializer, and untested a subscriber is a particular risk: it fails by going quiet, and a silent failure detector reads exactly like a healthy system. Thirteen tests, all passing on the first run; neither service was broken, both were unasserted. One asserts install is idempotent, because a second subscription would report every incident twice, and another passes a password in a payload and asserts it never reaches the emitted signal.

REAL_TOPIC_KEYS and TOPIC_GRADING both list the twelve real topics and are linked by a fetch that raises, so a topic added to one and not the other is a KeyError found by the first learner who opens it. An empty check list is worse: it grades every submission as a pass, because an empty array is all-true, and then divides by zero working out the score, so the learner is credited and immediately shown a 500. The guard for that divisor exists three method definitions away on the default grading path and not on the real-topic one. That asymmetry is deliberately left alone - whether a topic with no checks should pass, fail, or refuse to grade is a decision about grading and belongs to whoever owns the curriculum - but the table should never reach that state, and being a frozen constant it can only get there in a code change. Four invariants now fail there instead, including that every recorded solution passes its own topic's checks, which would otherwise let the course present an answer it marks wrong.

The repository states the English and Thai locale files must stay in sync and nothing checked it. Discipline had held - 2426 keys each, no difference in either direction - but this was the second stated invariant of the week being kept by hand rather than by a gate, and the first had already drifted by the time anybody looked. The failure does not announce itself: Rails is configured with fallbacks to English, so a key missing from Thai neither raises nor renders a translation-missing marker. It renders English to a reader who chose Thai, on a page that looks like it worked, and Thai is the default locale. Three checks, reading the two files rather than the I18n backend because the backend also carries the framework's English defaults. One empty Thai key was injected to confirm two of the three fire before the file was restored.

ADR-0048 decision 7 said an inactive organization is not reachable, the same way its other screens are not. The second clause was untrue when written: the work surface and the reporting page both refused a suspended company, while /company/:slug served a member its record normally, so the screen the decision was about was the strictest of the three rather than one of a set. The record refuses a member now. Administrators are a deliberate exception and a load-bearing one - /admin lists only active organizations and every membership action redirects back to this page, so refusing them too would let somebody suspend a company and leave no screen anywhere that could manage it. Decision 7 is amended rather than rewritten, keeping the original sentence with the correction underneath. This came out of an audit finding that was first reported backwards and withdrawn; reading the caller to withdraw it is what turned up that visible_to? has no status check at all.
